newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader ponders next move against deputies.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader ponders next move against deputies.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko ponders his next move on Saturday in his confrontation with the opposition-dominated parliament over a controversial referendum due next day.
Lukashenko wants to use the referendum to tighten his grip on rival institutions and extend his term by more than two years -- an idea fiercely opposed by parliament.
A compromise brokered by Russia looked close to collapse on Friday after parliament failed to approve it
After hours of angry debates, shouting and an ultimatum by Lukashenko to back the agreement by 6 p.m. (1600 GMT), deputies failed four times to approve it.
Lukashenko left the chamber, telling reporters he would consult the Russian leadership and his government and decide his next move on Saturday. Parliament adjourned until Tuesday.
Lukashenko, visiting parliament for the second time in the day, had bluntly told deputies late on Friday he would renege on the pact unless they backed it without further delay.

The row has many parallels with the crisis which paralysed politics in Russia for most of 1993 and ended in bloodshed when President Boris Yeltsin put down an armed revolt led by his parliamentary opponents.
Lukashenko, parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin signed an agreement at dawn on Friday after all-night talks to defuse the conflict.
The deal ran into trouble straight away on Friday morning when deputies dismissed it as a sell-out.
In Moscow, the Kremlin heralded it as a political masterstroke. "I consider this to be a big victory," said Yeltsin, adding the conflict could have ended in violence.
Yeltsin and the pro-Russian Lukashenko agreed last April to unite their countries in a loose community. But until three days ago, Moscow appeared reluctant to intervene in the conflict.
Under the Russian deal, Lukashenko has fallen in line with the constitutional court and parliament by cancelling decrees which made the referendum results legally binding.
In return, parliament and the court agreed to drop impeachment proceedings against him.

The two sides' referendum constitutional drafts -- one widening Lukashenko's powers and the other abolishing the presidency -- were to be put to a commission which would pass a new draft based on the results of the voting.
But Lukashenko will have a majority on the commission, and Western officials and his opponents have observed serious flaws in early voting which began almost two weeks ago on November 9.
